title: Not an Appointment
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass two
content:
Iroh invited Severus Snape to tea by sending him a formal card.

It was cream-colored, folded once, and bore a small green dragon stamped in the corner. The handwriting inside was beautiful.

Dear Professor Snape, it said. Your company would be welcome at the Jasmine Steps tasting on Thursday. No speeches are required.

Severus read the card twice.

Then he put it facedown on the kitchen table.

"Absolutely not."

I was cutting an apple into pieces small enough to eat while sorting a stack of invoices. I did not look up.

"Are you declining the tea or the lack of speeches?"

"The implication."

"Which implication?"

"That I have become a public exhibit."

I put down the apple knife. Severus had not discarded Iroh's card. For all his contempt of social obligations, he had placed it where he could see the green dragon on the fold.
"You can decline," I said. "He won't demand an explanation."
"I am aware how an invitation works."
"Then why are you glaring at it?"
He rested a finger on the handwriting. "Because I recognize someone accustomed to making a room comfortable even when the room has no right to ask it of him."
That caught me. "You think Iroh is performing?"
"I think he knows exactly when to be charming and when to stop. That is not the same thing."
I remembered the former general's voice turning hard when a real decision needed to be made. Severus had never been there. He had noticed the habit without pretending to share the man's history.
"Talk about tea," I suggested.
"Tea has soluble compounds. At least we could discuss something measurable."
"And if you enjoy the visit?"
"I shall conceal the scandal."
He moved the card an inch nearer. It was not yet a yes, and I did not steal one from his silence.
That evening he asked whether steeping temperature altered the bitterness of jasmine. I answered the actual question. His interest could belong to him without becoming my victory.

I set down the knife.

"He's inviting you to drink tea."

"He is inviting the notorious surviving spy of the war into a room full of people who think an interesting guest constitutes an evening's entertainment."

I folded the card and looked at the back. Nothing there suggested a lecture, a public question period, or a dramatic unveiling of Severus's biography.

"You could just say no," I said.

"I did."

"Then I'll tell him."

Severus turned toward me. He seemed almost disappointed by how easily I'd accepted his refusal.

"You intend to attend?"

"Yes. I like tea."

"An insufficient reason to subject yourself to crowds."

"I also like Iroh."

A small movement at the corner of his jaw told me he'd heard the choice of words. I gave him time to decide whether he wanted to ask the question behind it.

He did not.

I went back to my apple.

That was not the end of the argument.

It followed us through breakfast, into the annex, and all the way to Moonroot Archive. Severus insisted he was not offended. He was merely unimpressed by the presumption of strangers who thought they were entitled to his time.

I agreed that strangers were not entitled to his time.

He seemed to find this aggravating.

Near noon, Iroh arrived in the archive carrying a basket of clean cups for the pantry. He greeted Neri, complimented Pip on a repaired door latch, and came toward our worktable with a smile.

Iroh set the basket down and checked Mina's loan sheet. The count matched. He had brought back every cup that the pantry had agreed to lend.

Severus watched him with the suspicion he usually reserved for mislabeled ingredients.

"Are you delivering crockery or an argument?" he asked.

"Only the crockery, Professor. The argument would require a separate appointment."

I nearly laughed. Iroh's expression was pleasant, but not empty; he had the quick eyes of someone who had once made plans under much worse conditions than a crowded archive.

Neri signed for the cups. Iroh thanked them and folded the receipt. He didn't ask to see the historical records or make a claim on the workspace because he'd brought refreshments.

Severus tapped his pen against the table. "I presume this is not a surprise inspection."

"Not unless you have been brewing tea without a permit."

"There is no such permit."

"Excellent. Then we have avoided another form."

Mina's numbers remained on the cloth, and the cups went to their owners. Even a small gift or invitation, I thought, could arrive with its proper limits intact.

"I hope the card reached you," he said.

"It did," Severus answered.

"Good."

"I shall not be attending."

Iroh bowed his head slightly.

"Then I hope we may meet another day."

Severus looked as though someone had misplaced the rest of his argument.

"That is all?"

"Would you prefer a lengthy attempt to change your mind?"

"No."

"Then I shall spare us both."

Iroh turned to me.

"I will save a cup for anyone who arrives before the kettle cools. If you have time, Jasper, you are welcome."

"I'll be there."

"Wonderful."

He left the basket behind and went to help Mara set up the afternoon pantry shelves.

Severus stared after him.

"He is either genuinely polite or very skilled at appearing so."

"Both could be true."

"I dislike uncertainty."

"I've noticed."

The rest of the day was ordinary in ways that became important only later. We cataloged three damaged journals. Severus corrected a mislabeled vial and did not insult the apprentice who had made the error. Neri brought a photograph of the underside of the well's old stone arch, and we compared it with the drawing from the washed-up ledger fragment.

One line on the old map was blank.

Severus marked it, but did not guess what it meant.

Iroh returned for the basket he'd left behind just as Neri brought a second copy of the washed-up ledger map.

“Forgive the interruption,” he said. “Mara has discovered that an empty basket refuses to carry anything.”

Severus glanced at the basket. “A revelation for the ages.”

“I thought so.”

Neri spread the copy across the table. The blank line stopped just short of a dark mark near the lower maintenance passage. It might have been an erased signature. It might have been a damaged route label. A scholar had written in the margin that the mark showed where an old keeper had secretly opened the passage.

“That is unsupported,” Severus said immediately.

Iroh leaned closer, hands behind his back. “If it were a route marker, would it not be drawn toward a place someone expected to reach?”

“Only if we knew the mapmaker's notation. We don't.”

“And if it were a signature?”

“Then assigning an identity would be equally foolish.”

I waited for Iroh to make an elegant pronouncement. Instead he studied the faint ink and frowned as though he were examining a battle map he no longer trusted.

“In the war,” he said, “I have seen a general turn one uncertain line into a road because men were eager to march.”

Severus's expression changed. “A surprisingly rigorous observation.”

“Do not encourage him,” I told Severus. “He'll want to illustrate it with tea leaves.”

“I assure you,” Severus replied, “I require a specimen with a more predictable chemical structure.”

Neri raised one hand.

“Both of you. The ledger belongs to people who were denied the right to travel. I'd prefer our uncertainty be recorded before two clever men turn it into a contest.”

They were right. Severus made the annotation; Iroh signed as a reader who could confirm only what was visible on the copy. Neither claimed he knew the missing name. The original stayed protected, the lower passage stayed closed, and Neri decided which notes were suitable for public display.

Iroh collected his basket. “You would be welcome for tea another time, Professor.”

“And you,” Severus answered, “would be welcome to examine a properly labeled map.”

I nearly laughed. Neither of them seemed to realize that was their version of a friendly invitation.

At four o'clock, he closed his notebook.

"You should leave if you intend to be on time."

"Are you dismissing me?"

"I am observing the clock."

"That is how you dismissed me yesterday."

"Then you have learned to recognize a pattern."

I collected my bag and paused by the door.

"You could still come," I said. "Not because anyone expects you to be charming. Just because you might like the tea."

He looked at me for a long moment.

"I would not like the people."

"Then enjoy your evening without them."

His expression softened slightly.

"Do not let them make you stay beyond your wishes."

"I won't."

I went alone.

Jasmine Steps was crowded with the gentle noise of people who were not trying to impress one another. Greg had brought a guitar but was sitting with it unplayed across his knees. Katara was helping a neighbor carry a tray; Toph had occupied the chair with the best view of the garden despite not being interested in views.

Iroh poured a cup for me.

"Severus sends his regrets," I said.

"Does he?"

"More accurately, he sends an exceptionally firm no."

"Then I am glad he was able to give it."

We drank the tea. It tasted of mountain mint and something warm beneath it that I could not name.

After a while, Iroh asked how the archive was doing.

I told him about the mislabeled recipe, the corrected copy, and Neri's old drainage diagrams. I did not tell him which pages Severus had kept private. It felt good to speak about our work without opening the parts of it that did not belong to me.

Greg played a short melody after the cups were cleared. Toph complained that one note was half a beat late.

"That was on purpose," Greg said.

"Then you made a mistake intentionally. Congratulations."

Aang laughed so hard he nearly dropped his cup.

I stayed until the lanterns came on, then walked back toward Moonroot alone. I could have stayed longer. I could have gone to another person's door. My relationships did not turn every independent evening into evidence for or against anybody. I wanted to go home.

Severus was in the kitchen at Spinner's End when I arrived.

The kettle had already been filled.

"How was the exhibition?" he asked.

"Very disappointing. No one asked me to juggle, and nobody tried to turn me into a display."

"A shame."

"Greg played music."

"Predictable."

"Toph criticized the rhythm."

"An entirely reasonable response."

I hung up my coat.

"Did you have a good evening?"

"Quiet."

"Good."

He looked at me.

"That is all you intend to ask?"

"Did you want me to make an argument for attending next time?"

"No."

"Then I won't."

Severus set two mugs on the table. He hesitated before speaking.

"I considered that you might interpret my refusal as disinterest in the people you care about."

"I didn't."

"Or as a demand that you decline invitations on my behalf."

"I wouldn't."

He took a breath.

"I prefer to know where I stand."

"You stand wherever you choose, Severus. You don't need to attend every gathering. And I don't need to pretend everyone I love has identical boundaries."

Something in his shoulders eased.

"I could perhaps tolerate a smaller visit," he said. "At another time."

"Iroh would probably be delighted."

"Do not tell him I said delighted."

I smiled.

He moved toward me, paused, and lifted a hand to my cheek. His touch was careful, but there was nothing uncertain about the way he looked at me.

"May I?" he asked.

"Yes."

The kiss was brief, warm, and a little sharper when I smiled against his mouth. He rested his forehead against mine for one quiet beat.

The kettle began to whistle.

"That thing has the most appalling timing," I said.

"It has impeccable timing. You are simply distractible."

The tea was not as good as Iroh's.

I told Severus so.

He informed me that my palate remained beyond repair.

We drank it anyway, together at a table where neither of us had been required to prove love by being anywhere we didn't wish to be.
